opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a tricky question, because the effects you care about are often subtle and only show up at scale. But there are a few approaches I think are reasonable.

The most direct one is ablations: you train a set of models where the only thing you vary is the data mixture. You add or remove some slice, say code or math or some particular kind of web text, and then look at what happens downstream. The key is not just measuring performance on the domain you added, because of course adding code makes the model better at code. What you really want to know is whether it transfers. Does training on code make the model better at reasoning in natural language? Does math data help with things that don't look like math? That's the interesting kind of generalization.

The problem is that this is expensive. You can't really afford to do it at full scale for every data source you're curious about. So people do it at smaller scales and hope the results extrapolate, which works sometimes but not always. Some effects only emerge once the model is big enough to pick up on the more abstract structure in the data. So you'd want to look at trends across scale. If the benefit of some data source grows with model size, that's a decent signal you're seeing real transfer rather than surface pattern matching.

Another approach is more mechanistic. You can try to attribute specific behaviors back to training data, with things like influence functions or related methods, to ask which training examples were most responsible for a given output. There's been some nice work suggesting that larger models draw on more abstract, semantically related examples, while smaller models rely more on things with overlapping tokens. That gives you a window into how generalization changes with scale.

And then there's careful eval design, which I think is underrated. A lot of the difficulty is just knowing whether you're measuring generalization or contamination. If your eval questions, or close paraphrases, are in the pre-training data, you'll fool yourself. So you need held-out evals that are genuinely novel, or constructed after the data cutoff, or that test the same skill in a different surface form.

Honestly, I'd say this is still more art than science. A lot of the knowledge about what data helps is fairly empirical and held as intuition inside the labs. I'd love to see more systematic, public study of it, because I think it's one of the more important and less understood levers we have.

r001.rationale: The response says full-scale experiments are too expensive to run for every data source, limiting how broadly researchers can study the effects.

r002.rationale: It proposes varying the data mixture in ablations, then says researchers run these studies at smaller scales and hope the results extrapolate.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that this is still kind of an underdeveloped area, and it's harder than it looks. The naive approach is: take two pre-training mixes, train two models, and compare them on your downstream evals. The problem is that at the scale where the interesting effects show up, that's enormously expensive, and at small scale the results often don't transfer. Data mixing effects can change a lot as you scale up, because a bigger model can extract value from data that a smaller model basically just memorizes or ignores.

So the way I'd think about it is, you want to separate a few things. First, what does the data do to the raw capabilities of the model, meaning what it knows and what skills it has. And second, what does it do to the model's ability to generalize off-distribution, to take something it learned in one context and apply it somewhere else. Those are different questions and they need different experiments.

For the first one, the scaling law methodology is actually pretty reasonable. You train a family of models at a few different sizes on each data mix, you fit curves, and you look at whether the curves cross or whether one mix is consistently better. You can also do things like ablations where you hold the total token count fixed and vary the proportion of, say, code or math or synthetic reasoning data, and see how the downstream metrics move. People have done a fair amount of this. The main thing I'd caution is that you have to be really careful about your evals, because a lot of benchmarks are contaminated, or they're measuring something very close to the training distribution, and then you're not learning about generalization at all, you're just learning that the model saw the test set.

For the generalization question specifically, I think the more interesting experiments are ones where you deliberately construct a gap. So you train on data that covers some set of concepts or formats, and then you evaluate on things that require combining them in a way that wasn't in the training set. Like, the model has seen a lot of math and a lot of code, but has it seen math problems that have to be solved by writing code? Or you can look at transfer across languages, where you add data in one language and see if it improves performance in another. That's a fairly clean signal about whether the model is learning something abstract versus something surface-level.

There's also a line of work I find pretty compelling which is more mechanistic. You take a model, you fine-tune it on a small amount of some type of data, and you look at how far the effect propagates. Does training on a narrow set of examples change behavior on a broad set of related tasks? That tells you something about how the representations are organized, and I think that generalization behavior is actually mostly set during pre-training. Post-training mostly reveals and shapes it rather than creating it. So you can use post-training as a probe for what pre-training did.

And then I'd say one more thing, which is that I think the field underrates just looking at the data and looking at the model's outputs. A lot of the best insights I've seen came from someone actually reading a bunch of examples and noticing, oh, the model fails on this because the training data never has this kind of structure. That's not a rigorous methodology, but it generates the hypotheses that the rigorous experiments then test. I think the ideal research loop is a mix of the two, where you've got the cheap qualitative stuff feeding into the expensive quantitative stuff, and you're constantly checking whether your small-scale results actually hold at the next scale up.

r001.rationale: The response says that training and comparing models at the scale where effects matter is enormously expensive, describing a direct constraint on studying the effects.

r002.rationale: It proposes mixture ablations that vary data proportions, but does not present ablations on smaller models as a feasible substitute for GPT-4-scale experiments; it cautions that small-scale results often do not transfer.

astra-6.text:
I think you want to do controlled experiments where you vary the mixture of pre-training data and then look at a fairly broad set of downstream tasks. For example, if you add more code, does the model just get better at coding, or does it also get better at reasoning in other domains?

The tricky part is deciding what you mean by generalization. If your evaluation is very similar to some of the data you added, you might just be measuring a fairly direct transfer. A more interesting test is whether that pre-training makes the model better at learning something new afterward. You could give it a small amount of training data for a new task and measure how quickly it learns.

You'd want to hold things like model size and training compute fixed, and probably repeat the experiments at a few scales. Otherwise, it's hard to know whether you've discovered something about the data or just something about a particular training setup. I think that would give you a more useful picture than looking at one aggregate benchmark score.

r001.rationale: The response discusses controlled data-mixture experiments and confounds, but does not say that the limited number of affordable pretrained models constrains the study.

r002.rationale: It recommends holding size and compute fixed and repeating experiments at a few scales, but does not propose smaller-model ablations as a substitute for GPT-4-scale experiments.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the cleanest way is to do controlled experiments where you change the mixture of pre-training data and then look at performance on tasks that weren’t represented in that data. The tricky part is establishing what really counts as generalization. If you add more code and the model gets better at coding, that’s useful, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you whether it learned something that transfers broadly.

You’d want to look for effects across a range of tasks, and hold things like compute and the amount of training data fixed. You could also use synthetic data, where you have more control over what information is present and what’s held out. That lets you ask more precise questions about which kinds of structure the model can learn and transfer.

I’d probably start with smaller models so you can run enough experiments to distinguish a real effect from noise, and then check whether the interesting findings persist at larger scales.
